parsed.study_design: Cross-sectional community survey with direct interviews, structured questionnaires, observations, water-quality testing, and logistic regression
parsed.population_and_sample: 501 rural residents aged 13–55 from 13 communities in Isiala Ngwa North and South Local Government Areas, Abia State; 86% were women and children responsible for household water collection.
parsed.exposure: Deficient and uneven public water-service provision, including limited functionality of government/donor water projects, restricted pump operating hours, and community dependence on distant natural sources or private vendors.
parsed.outcome: Household water consumption relative to demand, distance and time required for collection, affordability constraints, service availability, and associated social, economic, educational, and health consequences.
parsed.rationale: Section 2 reports a systematic random cross-sectional survey of 501 residents, direct observation, water testing, and statistical analysis. Sections 2.1 and 3 document the administrative and institutional service conditions—only 8 of 18 public projects functioning, inconvenient operating hours, and unequal availability—and quantify outcomes including a mean 68% supply deficit, collection distance and time, and inability of some households to afford vendor water (pp. 410–415).
